newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels claims to have seized towns disputed.
newsitem.headline: Rebels claims to have seized towns disputed.

text.p: Rebels claimed to have seized a key town and parts of a major northeastern city in an apparent bid to sow panic among hundreds of Zairean government troops in them and prompt them to flee, U.N. sources said.

The rebels said on Tuesday they had captured Kindu town, an important stepping stone on the way to Kisangani city, which they claimed on Monday to have partially taken. A rebel officer backtracked on Tuesday, saying only that it was surrounded.
"They apparently want to prompt the Zairean troops to go on a last rampage of looting before fleeing," said a U.N. official, who has closely followed the rebel offensive since October.
"The rebels hope once the Zairean troops seize whatever they can carry they will flee, leaving rebel forces to walk in almost unchallenged -- as already happened in Uvira, Bukavu and Goma."
Residents of Kindu said by telephone on Wednesday that the town was still in government hands, and rebels were not in evidence.
They said Kindu, 400 km (250 miles) south of Kisangani, had been turned into a military fortress with the arrival of large numbers of Zairean soldiers.
The soldiers, unpaid for months and short of food, had done some limited looting there, the residents added.
The last two staff of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) pulled out of Kindu on security grounds on Wednesday, warning that thousands of people were without aid in the region.

"The ICRC expresses the strongest concern about the tens of thousands of civilians, displaced persons and refugees, without humanitarian aid for weeks in the region of Shabunda," an ICRC statement said.
Shabunda is 170 km (105 miles) east of Kindu and about halfway on the road from the eastern Zairean city of Bukavu, which was seized Tutsi Banyamulenge rebels in October.
A multinational force has been gathering in Uganda for the past two weeks but has so far been unable to bring any aid to Rwandan refugees and Zaireans in the east uprooted by fighting.

A senior State Department official said on Wednesday the United States was open to joining the international force if it had a clear mission, but Washington did not want to commit itself without knowing the whereabouts of the people it was supposed to help.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns, reflecting international concerns about the possible breakup of Zaire, said Washington opposed any partition of Zaire such as creation of a Tutsi-ruled state.

"The United States will not support in any way, shape, or form any effort by the rebel alliance to try to create any kind of artificial state in eastern Zaire or to deny to the government of Zaire its responsibilities in maintaining the international border with Rwanda and the other countries in central Africa and east Africa," Burns said in his daily briefing in Washington.
Residents of Kisangani, reached by radio on Tuesday, said Zairean authorities were trying to control hundreds of soldiers on the rampage after being defeated along the eastern borders of the country.
A Kisangani hotel was badly damaged on Tuesday when government forces trying to keep order attacked it with hand grenades in an assault on unruly troops who had been looting, they added.
Even without taking Kindu, the rebels hold a front 550 km (340 miles) long running north-south parallel to the border.
U.N. special envoy Raymond Chretien said on Wednesday that only Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko could solve the grave problems plaguing the Great Lakes region of Central Africa.

Speaking after meeting Mobutu at his luxury villa on the French Riviera where he is convalescing from cancer surgery, Chretien said the veteran leader had assured him he intended to play a role in solving the crisis.
In Burkina Faso, French President Jacques Chirac joined African leaders for a Franco-African summit overshadowed by the conflict in Zaire and repercussions on the Great Lakes region.
